planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep two weeks after the last frost; this 1997 Ambrose introduction was one of the earliest widely grown stellar-form dahlias.

directions: Camano Pet is an early stellar-form dahlia, introduced by hybridizer Dick Ambrose in 1997, with narrow quilled petals blending citrine yellow into soft cantaloupe tones on 5-inch blooms. Set tubers horizontally with the eye up once the soil has warmed after the last frost, spacing plants to let the four-foot stems branch freely. Pinch the center growing tip when plants reach about a foot tall to multiply bloom count, and stake before the flowering stems lean under their own weight. The twisting, well-spaced ray florets make it a favorite among growers looking for a true, early stellar form.
sources: American Dahlia Society — Stellar classification notes
Crazy 4 Dahlias — Camano Pet variety listing
Northwest Dahlia Legacy Project

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after soil has warmed; this 2017 Parshall introduction is among the largest-flowered stellar dahlias at up to 5 inches across.

directions: Clearview Del Sol, bred by Dick and Danielle Parshall and introduced in 2017, produces bright lemon-yellow stellar blooms up to 5 inches wide on sturdy four-foot stems, making it one of the larger-flowered members of the stellar class. Plant tubers horizontally with the sprout facing up once nights stay reliably above freezing. Pinch the growing tip early to encourage branching and feed lightly through the season, since the heavy bloom flush can stall without consistent moisture. Deadhead spent flowers regularly to keep the abundant yellow blooms coming from midsummer through the first frosts.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Dahlia 'Clearview Del Sol' plant profile
Crazy 4 Dahlias — Clearview Del Sol variety listing
American Dahlia Society — Stellar classification notes

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after danger of frost; this 2013 Paul Bloomquist Legacy Collection introduction shifts from gold and orange to deeper rust tones as days shorten.

directions: Bloomquist Pumpkin, part of Washington hybridizer Paul Bloomquist's Legacy Collection and introduced in 2013, carries layered orange and golden-yellow stellar blooms 4 to 6 inches across that deepen toward rust as autumn approaches. Plant tubers horizontally with the eye up once the soil has warmed, allowing 12 to 18 inches between plants for the bushy four-foot habit. Pinch young plants to encourage branching and stake before stems lean under the weight of the long-stemmed blooms. Cut flowers when three-quarters open for the best vase life, and keep picking to extend the bloom season into fall.
sources: Floret Flower Farm — Dahlia Bloomquist Pumpkin variety notes
Triple Wren Farms — Bloomquist Pumpkin growing comparison
Dahlia Hill Garden — Bloomquist Pumpkin portfolio entry

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after soil has warmed; stake early since this Derrill W. Hart Award-winning stellar type produces heavy 7-inch blooms on 5-6 foot plants.

directions: Gitts Crazy, bred by Nicholas Gitts, won the American Dahlia Society's Derrill W. Hart Award as a top-scoring new stellar-form dahlia, with long involute petals opening golden-bronze and curling back to reveal a rosy-purple reverse. Plant tubers horizontally with the eye up after the last frost, giving plants extra room since mature clumps can reach six feet. Stake early and often, since the 7-inch blooms are heavy for the stem, and pinch the lead shoot when young to build a stronger branching framework. Expect the two-toned gold-and-magenta color show to intensify from midsummer into early autumn.
sources: American Dahlia Society — Derrill W. Hart Award records
Swan Island Dahlias — Gitts Crazy variety listing

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after frost danger passes; this 2018 Les Connell introduction sets very few tubers, so divide clumps conservatively in fall.

directions: Tahoma Stellar Feller, introduced by Les Connell in 2018, bears pearly ivory stellar blooms 5 to 6 inches across with a soft mauve blush and slightly darker centers, held on tall, long stems well suited to cutting. Plant tubers horizontally with the eye up once soil has warmed, and expect modest tuber increase at season's end since this cultivar is a notoriously light producer. Stake the tall stems early and pinch young plants to encourage side branching for more flowers. Harvest blooms when three-quarters open for the longest vase life.
sources: Floret Flower Farm — Dahlia Tahoma Stellar Feller variety notes
Connell's Dahlias
Idlewild Blooms

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after the last frost and stake early; this Kristine Albrecht introduction (bred 2019) can reach over 5 feet and sets seed readily.

directions: KA's Champagne, bred by Kristine Albrecht, offers creamy champagne-toned stellar blooms about 4 inches across, blushed with soft pink and warmed by a buttery-yellow base. Plant tubers horizontally with the eye facing up once soil has warmed, and stake plants early since mature stems can top five feet under the bloom load. Pinch young growth to build branching structure and remove spent flowers often to keep new buds forming. This vigorous grower is also an unusually generous seed producer, making it a useful parent for home hybridizing.
sources: Stonehollow Farmstead — KA's Champagne variety notes
The Dahlia Hub — KA's Champagne variety profile
Crazy 4 Dahlias — KA's Champagne listing

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after frost danger passes; this dwarf single-flowered mignon type needs no staking and suits pots or border fronts.

directions: G.F. Hemerik is a classic Dutch mignon single dahlia dating to 1936, bearing masses of coppery-orange, single flowers roughly 3 inches across with eight broad, soft-tipped petals around a prominent yellow disc. Its compact 16 to 18 inch habit needs no staking, making it ideal for container growing or the front of a border. Plant tubers horizontally in well-drained soil once the ground has warmed after the last frost, and deadhead regularly to keep the massed bloom display going from midsummer until frost. Because stems are relatively weak, it performs better as a garden plant than as a cut flower.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden — Plant Finder, Dahlia 'G.F. Hemerik'
Old House Gardens — G.F. Hemerik dahlia history

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 3-4 inches deep after the last frost; this dark-foliaged dwarf mignon single, registered 1991, suits containers and needs no support.

directions: Scura is a dwarf mignon single dahlia with fiery red-orange blooms 1 to 4 inches wide set against handsome near-black foliage, part of the compact Topmix group of bedding dahlias. Plant tubers horizontally in free-draining soil once nights stay reliably above freezing, and skip staking since the sturdy habit stays under 16 inches tall. It forms a tidy, floriferous mound that blooms for months, making it a strong choice for pots, window boxes, or the front edge of a sunny border. Deadhead spent blooms to keep new single flowers coming through the season.
sources: Shoot Gardening — Dahlia 'Scura' plant profile
Royal Horticultural Society

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed; this anemone-flowered type pairs a dense yellow pincushion center with striped magenta-and-white outer petals.

directions: Boogie Woogie is an anemone-flowered dahlia whose flat outer petals of magenta-pink and white frame a domed, powder-puff center of short, toothed golden-yellow florets. Plant tubers horizontally with the eye up after the last frost, in loamy, well-drained soil in full sun. Pinch the growing tip when plants are young to promote bushier branching and more of the distinctive pincushion blooms. Lift and store tubers after the first hard frost in colder climates, since this cultivar is not reliably winter-hardy outside mild zones.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Dahlia 'Boogie Woogie' plant profile
Bluestone Perennials — Dahlia Boogie Woogie variety notes

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after frost danger passes and stake immediately; this 1993 Ed Redd giant formal decorative can carry 6-10 inch blooms on 5.5 foot stems.

directions: Elma Elizabeth is a giant formal decorative dahlia introduced in 1993 by hybridizer Ed Redd, producing fully double blooms 6 to 10 inches across in layered deep pink and lavender tones with darker purple highlights. Set tubers horizontally with the eye up once soil has warmed, and drive stakes at planting time since the five-and-a-half-foot stems carry heavy blooms that need support from early in the season. Disbud side shoots around the terminal flower bud if show-size blooms are the goal, and water deeply and consistently through summer to sustain the large flower size. Feed moderately, since excess nitrogen will favor foliage over the giant dinnerplate-class flowers.
sources: Draginas Dahlias — Elma Elizabeth variety notes
Idlewild Blooms — Elma Elizabeth dahlia tuber listing

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed; this dark-red orchid-form dahlia reaches about 4 feet and shares its naming line with the Bloomquist decorative series.

directions: Bloomquist Trophy is an orchid-form dahlia carrying a single row of deep red, narrowly involute petals rolled along their length around a tight central disc. Plant tubers horizontally with the eye facing up once the soil has warmed after the last frost, spacing plants to let the four-foot habit fill in without crowding. Pinch the central growing tip early to build a branching framework with more flowering stems, and stake before the plant reaches full height. The narrow, quill-like petals give the blooms an airy, open look that stands out against bulkier decorative types nearby in the border.
sources: North Cascade Dahlias — Bloomquist Trophy variety listing
American Dahlia Society — Orchid classification notes

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed; this laciniated (fringed-petal) novelty type produces frilly 4-6 inch orange blooms.

directions: Mel's Orange Marmalade belongs to the laciniated, or fringed, novelty dahlias, in which each petal splits at the tip into fine, frayed divisions that give the bright orange, 4 to 6 inch blooms a feathery, sea-anemone-like texture quite different from the smooth-edged decorative and ball classes. Plant tubers horizontally with the eye up once the soil has warmed after the last frost, and provide a stake for the three to four foot stems before they lean under the bloom's weight. Pinch young plants to encourage bushier growth and more flowering stems, and deadhead regularly to keep the profuse, ruffled blooms coming through late summer. The fringed petal texture reads especially well in close-up garden plantings or cut arrangements.
sources: Gardenia.net — Dahlia 'Mel's Orange Marmalade' plant profile
Todd's Botanics — Dahlia 'Mel's Orange Marmalade' listing
